item.passage: Editors long treated Emily Dickinson's dashes as accidents of a private hand—marks a tidy publisher could safely regularize into commas and periods. The impulse is understandable. Dickinson never prepared her poems for print, and her manuscripts bristle with slashes of varying length and angle that resist any consistent grammatical rule. One might conclude that the dashes carry no deliberate meaning. But irregularity is not the same as randomness. Close study of the fascicles reveals that the marks cluster at moments of semantic hinge—where a line could pivot toward two incompatible readings—and there they do a work no comma could: they suspend the reader between meanings rather than resolving them. What the editors mistook for a defect to be corrected was in fact Dickinson's most precise instrument. The dashes do not fail to punctuate; they punctuate a kind of thought that standard marks were never designed to hold.
item.explanation: The passage states the editors' view of the dashes as accidents, concedes why that impulse was understandable, then pivots on 'But irregularity is not the same as randomness' to reread the same marks as deliberate. That is the structure that 'presents a longstanding interpretation, grants the conditions that made it plausible, and then overturns it by reinterpreting the same evidence.' The structure in which editors 'gradually came to appreciate their deliberate artistry' is the trap: nobody in the passage changes their mind, the author simply argues against them. The structure that 'weighs two competing schools of modern criticism' invents a debate the text never stages. And the structure claiming the dashes must be preserved because Dickinson's 'intentions can never be recovered' reverses the conclusion, which is that the dashes are her most precise instrument and their purpose legible.
item.correct_answer: It presents a longstanding interpretation, grants the conditions that made it plausible, and then overturns it by reinterpreting the same evidence.

distractor_rationales.choice: It traces how editors gradually came to appreciate the deliberate artistry of Dickinson's punctuation.
It contrasts two competing schools of modern criticism regarding Dickinson's manuscripts.
It argues that Dickinson's dashes should be preserved because her intentions are ultimately unknowable.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's characterization of the shift to agriculture?

The earliest farming settlements were far larger and more densely settled than the forager camps that preceded them on the same land.
Skeletons from the first farming communities show greater height and fewer stress markers than neighboring foragers'.

item.passage: The transition to agriculture is routinely narrated as an obvious upgrade: farming produced more food, so foragers naturally adopted it. Skeletal evidence complicates the story. The bones of early farmers show, relative to the foragers who preceded them, shorter stature, more dental disease, and more markers of nutritional stress—hardly the profile of a population that had traded up. Agriculture did yield more calories per acre, but those calories came from a narrower range of starchy staples, purchased with longer labor and denser settlement that bred infection. Why, then, did anyone farm? The likeliest answer is not that farming was better but that, once populations had grown around it, returning to foraging could no longer feed them. Agriculture may have been less a prize that foragers seized than a trap that closed behind them—advantageous to the group's numbers even as it diminished the individual's health.
item.explanation: The author's characterization is that farming was a trap: good for the group's numbers, bad for the individuals, with the skeletal record supplying the evidence of that individual cost. Skeletons from the first farming communities showing "greater height and fewer stress markers than neighboring foragers" would reverse that evidence and pull the load-bearing support out from under the claim. The strongest trap is the finding that early crops "delivered several times more calories per acre" than wild foods - it feels like a refutation, but the passage already concedes the caloric advantage and denies that it translated into individual well-being. The observation that the earliest farming settlements "were far larger and more densely settled" than the camps before them fits the argument, since denser settlement is one of the costs the author names. And the fact that some forager groups "declined to take up agriculture for many centuries" bears on how fast farming spread, not on whether farmers were healthier.
item.correct_answer: Skeletons from the first farming communities show greater height and fewer stress markers than neighboring foragers'.

distractor_rationales.choice: Some forager groups living beside farmers declined to adopt agriculture for many centuries.
The earliest farming settlements were larger and more densely populated than forager camps.
Early crops delivered more calories per acre than the wild foods gathered from the same land.

item.prompt: What is the main rhetorical purpose of the passage?

item.passage: A popular history casts the acceptance of continental drift as a simple triumph of evidence over stubborn dogma: Wegener was right, his critics were blinkered, and the fossils vindicated him. The truth is less flattering to hindsight. Wegener's contemporaries rejected his theory not out of mere prejudice but because he could specify no plausible mechanism—no force strong enough to plow continents through solid ocean floor—and the mechanism he did propose was demonstrably too weak. Their skepticism was, by the evidential standards of the day, reasonable. Drift was ultimately accepted only when seafloor spreading supplied the missing mechanism decades later. To celebrate Wegener as a lone visionary crushed by dogmatists is thus to misdescribe the episode: it was not that his critics ignored good reasoning, but that the reasoning available to everyone, Wegener included, was genuinely incomplete.
item.explanation: The passage recasts the heroic story: Wegener's contemporaries rejected drift because he 'could specify no plausible mechanism,' and their skepticism was 'reasonable' by the evidential standards of the day. That is the answer that revises a heroic narrative by showing that the resistance reflected a real evidential gap rather than closed-mindedness. The answer that Wegener's critics were driven by professional dogma, and that the popular history has understated how much prejudice shaped their resistance, reverses the passage, which defends them as reasoning well from what was available. The answer that the fossil evidence marshalled on Wegener's behalf was never strong enough to establish that the continents had once been joined overreads: the correspondences are treated as genuine and ultimately vindicated, the gap being mechanism rather than evidence. And the answer that Wegener himself anticipated seafloor spreading is contradicted - that mechanism arrived decades later, from other hands.

A more searching reading reverses the charge. The genre's obsessive returns to imprisonment, inheritance, and the tyranny of the dead over the living, this reading holds, registered anxieties that Enlightenment optimism could not voice directly: about property, patriarchal authority, and a past that would not stay buried. The ghosts, on this account, are not a flight from the period's preoccupations but a coded confrontation with them. What looks like the genre's silliest feature—its refusal to let the supernatural be fully explained away—becomes its most serious, a way of insisting that some fears resist rational dissolution.

The option that it "defends the traditional view that the Gothic novel was escapist" reverses the argument, which overturns that view rather than upholding it. Figures such as Robert Boyle did champion experiment, but they also leaned heavily on the testimony of credible witnesses—gentlemen whose social standing, not any repeatable procedure, vouched for what they reported. The novelty of the age, then, lay less in a rejection of authority than in a redefinition of whose authority counted. The learned commentator on Aristotle was displaced not by the anonymous fact but by the trustworthy observer, a figure whose reliability was itself a social construction. What looks in retrospect like the birth of impersonal objectivity was in practice the substitution of one hierarchy of credibility for another—a shift real enough, but far more modest than the heroic narrative of liberated reason suggests.

item.prompt: How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the distinction Text 1 draws between fluency and comprehension?

A system might manipulate symbols according to rules—matching outputs to inputs flawlessly—while grasping the meaning of none of them. Fluency is not comprehension; a convincing performance of understanding can be wholly hollow, a matter of syntax without semantics.

Its author would therefore answer Text 1 by arguing that once performance is flexible and reliable enough, there is no further comprehension left for it to lack. The option that has Text 2 "conceding that a system matching outputs to inputs by rule cannot thereby understand" anything restates Text 1's own thesis and puts it in the wrong author's mouth. The option in which Text 2 agrees conversational tests are too easy and proposes "a more demanding behavioral standard" misses the disagreement: Text 2 does not want a stricter test for detecting a hidden state, it denies that there is a hidden state to detect. And the option predicting that "machines will in time acquire the inner semantics" whose absence Text 1 laments accepts Text 1's framing and merely postpones the problem, whereas Text 2 rejects the missing ingredient altogether.

item.prompt: The author would most likely regard a scientist who responds to a failed prediction by revising an auxiliary assumption as
choices: not necessarily unscientific, since one such revision does not amount to shielding a theory from all refutation.
clearly unscientific, since a theory that escapes a failed prediction by adjusting an assumption no longer forbids any observation.
scientific only if the core theory is eventually abandoned once enough anomalies have accumulated.

item.passage: Popper's criterion—that a theory is scientific only if it forbids some observation—remains the textbook badge of science, and it captures something real: a theory compatible with every conceivable result explains nothing. Yet the criterion is cleaner in principle than in practice. No theory confronts evidence alone; it arrives escorted by auxiliary assumptions about instruments, initial conditions, and background laws. When a prediction fails, logic alone cannot say whether the theory or one of its escorts is at fault, and scientists rationally often revise an escort rather than discard a fruitful core. A doctrine that shielded itself indefinitely by such maneuvers would indeed be pseudoscience; but a theory that survives one anomaly by adjusting an assumption has not thereby cheated. Falsifiability marks a real difference in spirit—an openness to refutation—without providing the mechanical test Popper's admirers imagine. It is a virtue to cultivate, not a rule to apply.
item.explanation: The passage separates one rational revision from a policy of endless evasion: because a theory never meets evidence without auxiliary assumptions, logic alone cannot say which link failed, and "a theory that survives one anomaly by adjusting an assumption has not thereby cheated." The author would therefore call such a scientist not necessarily unscientific. The option calling the move "clearly unscientific" because the theory "no longer forbids any observation" applies the mechanical Popperism the passage spends its length qualifying; it is the strongest trap. The option that the scientist counts as scientific "only if the core theory is eventually abandoned" once anomalies accumulate imposes a threshold the passage never sets - falsifiability is called a virtue to cultivate, not a rule to apply. And the option that the scientist is "engaged in exactly the" indefinite self-shielding that marks pseudoscience collapses the very distinction the passage is built on, between one revision and a doctrine that shields itself forever.

item.prompt: The author of Text 2 would most likely argue that the reasoning in Text 1 fails because it

Text 1
Automation anxiety rests on a simple arithmetic: a machine that does a worker's task eliminates that worker's job, so each advance in automation subtracts from total employment. On this logic, the accelerating capability of machines forecasts a future of vanishing work.

Text 2
Historically, that arithmetic has failed to hold. Automating a task lowers the cost of the good or service it produces; cheaper output expands demand, and the same firms often hire more people—for tasks the machines cannot do—than the automation displaced. The net effect on employment has usually been positive, not because machines create no losers, but because the displaced-worker calculation ignores the demand that falling prices unleash. Whether this pattern will continue is a separate question; the point is only that the subtraction model has been historically wrong about the total.

The answer that Text 1 wrongly denies that any workers at all are displaced misreads both texts - Text 1 asserts displacement, and Text 2 grants that 'machines create losers.' The answer that Text 1 assumes that machines will eventually match every human capability names a premise Text 1 never states and Text 2 never attacks; Text 2's counterexample is precisely the tasks machines cannot do. And the answer that Text 1 assumes without argument that the historical pattern of offsetting hiring is certain to continue points at the wrong text: continued offsetting is what Text 2 itself calls 'a separate question.'
item.correct_answer: ignores how falling production costs can expand demand and create offsetting employment.

item.prompt: Based on the passage, it can most reasonably be inferred that a nineteenth-century listener would most likely have regarded a soloist who played only the notes as written as

item.passage: We tend to imagine the classical concert as the faithful realization of a fixed text, the performer a servant of the score. Historically this is an anachronism. Well into the nineteenth century, notation was understood as a scaffold, not a blueprint: soloists were expected to improvise cadenzas, ornament melodies, even recompose passages in performance, and a player who reproduced the notes mechanically would have seemed not scrupulous but deficient. The modern reverence for the “work” as an inviolable object is itself a historical artifact, consolidated only as concerts became museums of the past. None of this means the score was dispensable—it constrained and guided what the performer could do. But it named a space for invention rather than closing one, and to perform such music “authentically” today may require the very freedoms our fidelity has taught us to suppress.

The option describing the soloist as "disregarding the score," treating it as "dispensable once a performer begins to invent," misreports the text, which insists the score was not dispensable and that it constrained and guided what the performer could do. And the option calling the player "unusually accomplished" because cadenzas and ornaments "were rare until the twentieth century" inverts the history: improvisation was the expectation then, and strict fidelity is the later development.

MOND requires far more adjustable parameters than the dark-matter hypothesis does.
item.passage:
Text 1
Galaxies rotate too rapidly to be held together by the gravity of their visible matter alone; their outermost stars ought to fly off into space, yet they remain bound. The dominant explanation posits vast halos of unseen 'dark matter,' whose additional gravity supplies the missing pull. Though never detected directly, dark matter coheres with a remarkably wide range of independent cosmological observations.

Text 2
An alternative dispenses with dark matter altogether. Modified Newtonian Dynamics, or MOND, proposes that gravity itself behaves differently at very low accelerations, growing stronger than Newton's law predicts. With a single adjusted parameter, MOND reproduces the rotation curves of individual galaxies with striking accuracy—frequently outperforming dark-matter models. It falters, however, at larger scales, struggling to account for the behavior of galaxy clusters and for conditions in the early universe.
item.explanation: Text 2 itself concedes that MOND falters at galaxy clusters and in the early universe, while Text 1 stresses dark matter's fit with a wide range of independent observations — so the strongest counter is the point that MOND, 'though successful for individual galaxies, fails to explain the larger-scale phenomena that dark matter accommodates.' The counter that MOND 'cannot reproduce the rotation curves of individual galaxies as accurately' is contradicted by Text 2, which says it frequently outperforms dark-matter models there. The counter that 'dark matter has been directly observed' is false on Text 1's own terms, since Text 1 calls it never detected directly. And the counter that MOND 'requires far more adjustable parameters' is contradicted by Text 2's single adjusted parameter.
item.correct_answer: Text 2's account, though successful for individual galaxies, fails to explain the larger-scale phenomena that dark matter accommodates.

distractor_rationales.choice: MOND cannot reproduce the rotation curves of individual galaxies as accurately as dark-matter models can.
Dark matter has been directly observed, whereas MOND's proposed modification has not.
MOND requires far more adjustable parameters than the dark-matter hypothesis does.

item.prompt: The relationship between the two texts is best described as
choices: Text 2 supplies comparative historical examples that confirm Text 1's thesis that a consensus on fundamental values steadies a democracy.
Text 2 challenges Text 1 by relocating the source of democratic durability from shared values to practiced habits of compromise.
Text 2 agrees with Text 1 that shared values are the foundation of democratic durability but adds that institutions must actively enforce them.
Text 2 argues that democracies rarely survive serious crises at all, whatever their value consensus or their habits of institutional compromise.
item.passage:
Text 1: A resilient democracy, many theorists hold, requires a broad consensus on fundamental values. Where citizens share deep commitments, they can weather disagreement on policy, because a common moral foundation keeps conflict from becoming existential. Shared values, on this view, are the ballast that steadies the ship of state.

Text 2: Bermeo's comparative work suggests the ballast metaphor misleads. The democracies that most reliably survived crises were not those with the deepest value consensus but those with dense institutional habits of compromise—coalitions, power-sharing, routines of bargaining. Some highly consensual societies fractured quickly once a single divisive issue arose, precisely because they had little practice negotiating across real disagreement. Durability, she argues, is built less by agreeing on ends than by rehearsing the procedures for living with disagreement about them.
item.explanation: Text 1 makes shared fundamental values the ballast of a stable democracy; Bermeo's comparison says the ballast metaphor misleads and puts durability in "dense institutional habits of compromise" instead, noting that some highly consensual societies fractured quickly for want of practice at negotiating. Relocating the source of durability from shared values to practiced compromise is the relationship the key names. The option that Text 2 "supplies comparative historical examples that confirm" Text 1 gets the direction backwards - those examples are counterexamples. The option that Text 2 agrees shared values are foundational "but adds that institutions must actively enforce them" is the trap for readers who expect paired texts to converge; Bermeo does not enforce the consensus, she replaces it as the explanation. And the option that "democracies rarely survive serious crises at all" contradicts the premise of her comparison, which is precisely that some of them reliably did.
item.correct_answer: Text 2 challenges Text 1 by relocating the source of democratic durability from shared values to practiced habits of compromise.

distractor_rationales.choice: Text 2 supplies comparative historical examples that confirm Text 1's thesis that a consensus on fundamental values steadies a democracy.
Text 2 agrees with Text 1 that shared values are the foundation of democratic durability but adds that institutions must actively enforce them.
Text 2 argues that democracies rarely survive serious crises at all, whatever their value consensus or their habits of institutional compromise.

item.prompt: Which choice is the most reasonable inference from the passage?
choices: Once a memory has been reconsolidated for the first time, it is permanently fixed and cannot be altered by any later retrieval, however surprising the circumstances.
The more frequently a memory is retrieved, the more distorted it grows, since each recall returns the trace to a labile state in which change is inevitable.
Prediction errors are the only mechanism by which a long-term memory is first formed, so a memory encoded without surprise never stabilizes at all.
A memory recalled in circumstances identical to those in which it was formed is unlikely to be altered by the act of recall.
item.passage: The metaphor of memory as a recording implies that each act of recall simply replays a fixed trace. Reconsolidation research complicates this picture, but not in the way popular accounts suggest. It is often reported that 'every time you remember something, you change it'—as though memory were hopelessly plastic. What the experiments actually show is narrower: retrieving a consolidated memory returns it, briefly, to a labile state in which it can be modified before it restabilizes, but only under specific conditions—a mismatch between the expected and the encountered, for instance. Absent such a prediction error, the reactivated memory reconsolidates essentially unchanged. Plasticity, in other words, is gated: the brain updates a memory only when new information signals that the old version is incomplete. The system is thus better described as conservative than as fickle, revising its records not promiscuously but when, and only when, the world has given it reason to.
item.explanation: Modification requires a prediction error—a mismatch between expected and encountered. Identical circumstances supply no mismatch, so the memory reconsolidates 'essentially unchanged.' The tempting trap is the popular 'recall distorts memory' claim, which the passage explicitly narrows and rejects. The 'permanently fixed' option contradicts the text (retrieval re-opens a labile state), and the 'prediction errors form memory' option confuses updating an existing memory with initial formation—a scope error the passage never licenses.
item.correct_answer: A memory recalled in circumstances identical to those in which it was formed is unlikely to be altered by the act of recall.

distractor_rationales.choice: Once a memory has been reconsolidated for the first time, it is permanently fixed and cannot be altered by any later retrieval, however surprising the circumstances.
The more frequently a memory is retrieved, the more distorted it grows, since each recall returns the trace to a labile state in which change is inevitable.
Prediction errors are the only mechanism by which a long-term memory is first formed, so a memory encoded without surprise never stabilizes at all.

item.prompt: The main rhetorical purpose of the passage's final sentence is to
choices: dismiss standard economic theory as incapable of predicting how any wage floor will affect employment.
concede that the competitive model correctly describes the great majority of labor markets.
present monopsony as an odd exception that leaves the textbook prediction essentially intact.
recast the puzzling evidence as a challenge to one assumption rather than to economic theory itself.
item.passage: Introductory textbooks present a clean verdict: a minimum wage set above the market rate must reduce employment, since firms hire only up to the point where a worker's wage equals the value she adds. Empirical studies of actual wage floors, however, have repeatedly failed to detect the predicted job losses, and some find modest employment gains. The textbook model assumes that employers are price-takers who cannot influence the wage they pay. But where a few firms dominate local hiring, they face an upward-sloping labor supply curve and can suppress wages below the competitive level. In such 'monopsonistic' markets, a minimum wage can raise pay and employment simultaneously, because it removes the incentive to restrict hiring in order to hold wages down. The anomalous findings, then, need not overturn economic theory; they expose the narrowness of the assumption on which the textbook prediction silently depends.
item.explanation: The final sentence says the findings 'need not overturn economic theory' but 'expose the narrowness of the assumption' about price-taking employers—exactly the relocation the answer describes, “a challenge to one assumption rather than to economic theory itself”. The choice “dismiss standard economic theory” is the misreading the sentence explicitly blocks ('need not overturn'). The choice “concede that the competitive model correctly describes” is unsupported: the passage never claims the competitive model fits most markets. The choice “present monopsony as an odd exception” wrongly frames monopsony as a minor exception, whereas the passage treats the price-taking assumption itself as the flaw.
item.correct_answer: recast the puzzling evidence as a challenge to one assumption rather than to economic theory itself.

distractor_rationales.choice: dismiss standard economic theory as incapable of predicting how any wage floor will affect employment.
concede that the competitive model correctly describes the great majority of labor markets.
present monopsony as an odd exception that leaves the textbook prediction essentially intact.

item.prompt: Based on the text, it can most reasonably be inferred that the author regards the 1890 edition's editorial changes as
choices: regrettable distortions whose harm to Dickinson's reputation outweighed any benefit they produced
evidence that Dickinson had actively sought a wide contemporary readership during her lifetime
a necessary precondition for the later appreciation of Dickinson's unaltered work
the primary reason her poems were ignored during her lifetime
item.passage: The familiar account of Emily Dickinson casts her as a misunderstood visionary whose radical prosody baffled contemporaries and languished until modern readers could appreciate it. Yet the archival record complicates this romance. Dickinson circulated hundreds of poems privately, and correspondents praised them; her obscurity was less a verdict than a preference. When Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Higginson prepared the 1890 edition, they smoothed her dashes into conventional punctuation and supplied titles—alterations later scholars deplored as vandalism. But those very emendations, by rendering the verse legible to Victorian taste, secured the wide readership that made an unedited Dickinson thinkable at all. The poet we now prize for her jagged singularity reached us first in domesticated form. To credit her belated canonization solely to a modern sensibility, then, is to mistake the effect for the cause: the audience capable of valuing her strangeness was one that her editors' compromises had helped to create.
item.explanation: The passage reports that later scholars deplored the 1890 emendations as vandalism, then reverses the verdict: smoothing the dashes and supplying titles 'secured the wide readership that made an unedited Dickinson thinkable at all.' So the author regards them as a necessary precondition for the later appreciation of Dickinson's unaltered work. The answer calling them regrettable distortions whose harm to Dickinson's reputation outweighed any benefit stops at the scholars' verdict and drops the author's rebuttal - the intuitive trap. The answer treating them as evidence that Dickinson had actively sought a wide contemporary readership contradicts the claim that her obscurity 'was less a verdict than a preference.' And the answer making them the primary reason her poems were ignored during her lifetime breaks the chronology: the edition appeared in 1890, after her death, so it cannot explain neglect while she lived.
item.correct_answer: a necessary precondition for the later appreciation of Dickinson's unaltered work

distractor_rationales.choice: regrettable distortions whose harm to Dickinson's reputation outweighed any benefit they produced
evidence that Dickinson had actively sought a wide contemporary readership during her lifetime
the primary reason her poems were ignored during her lifetime

item.prompt: Which statement about writing systems is best supported by the passage?
choices: By fixing a standard spelling, writing systems tend to keep a language's pronunciation more stable than that of comparable unwritten languages.
Writing systems can influence pronunciation less by resisting change than by supplying older forms that speakers may later revive.
Languages with writing systems ultimately undergo fewer total sound changes than languages without them.
Spelling pronunciation occurs because literate speakers consciously prefer archaic forms to innovative ones.
item.passage: It is often assumed that a language's writing system slows the pace at which its spoken form changes, anchoring pronunciation to a fixed orthographic standard. The historical record complicates this assumption. In several literate societies, sound changes proceeded at rates indistinguishable from those in neighboring unwritten languages; the spelling simply drifted out of alignment with speech, as English orthography notoriously has. What writing does appear to preserve is not pronunciation but the memory of older forms, which remain available to be reactivated. Speakers who encounter an archaic spelling may, generations after a sound has shifted, reintroduce a pronunciation closer to the written form—a phenomenon called spelling pronunciation. Writing, on this view, does not brake change so much as widen the range of variants a community can draw on, occasionally reversing a completed shift precisely because the discarded form was never fully discarded from the page.
item.explanation: The passage denies that writing brakes sound change and says instead that it preserves older forms which remain available to be reactivated — the statement that writing influences pronunciation 'less by resisting change than by supplying older forms that speakers may later revive.' The statement that a standard spelling keeps pronunciation 'more stable than that of comparable unwritten languages' is the very assumption the passage says the historical record complicates, and is the prime trap. The statement that literate languages 'undergo fewer total sound changes' overgeneralizes into a tally the passage never makes; it reports rates indistinguishable from unwritten neighbors. And the statement that spelling pronunciation occurs because speakers 'consciously prefer archaic forms' attributes a deliberate taste, whereas the passage describes only the reactivation of variants that the page kept available.
item.correct_answer: Writing systems can influence pronunciation less by resisting change than by supplying older forms that speakers may later revive.

distractor_rationales.choice: By fixing a standard spelling, writing systems tend to keep a language's pronunciation more stable than that of comparable unwritten languages.
Languages with writing systems ultimately undergo fewer total sound changes than languages without them.
Spelling pronunciation occurs because literate speakers consciously prefer archaic forms to innovative ones.

item.prompt: The passage most strongly implies that the "sheepskin effect" is difficult to reconcile with
choices: the signaling claim that a credential certifies the diligence and ability employers cannot observe.
the observation that workers with more schooling tend to earn more than those with less.
a pure human-capital account in which wages track only the skills acquired through coursework.
the finding that workers who leave one year short of a degree still out-earn those who never enrolled.
item.passage: The human-capital account holds that education raises wages because it makes workers more productive. The signaling account offers a rival mechanism: schooling raises wages chiefly by certifying pre-existing traits—diligence, conformity, raw ability—that employers cannot observe directly. The two are notoriously hard to separate, since both predict that the educated earn more. One wedge is the 'sheepskin effect': the disproportionate wage jump associated with completing a degree's final year and receiving the credential, over and above the return to the years of coursework themselves. If a diploma paid only for the skills acquired, the last year should pay about like the others. That it pays more suggests part of education's return flows not from what is learned but from what the credential certifies. The effect does not refute human capital; it merely shows that certification does some of the work the productivity story claims for skill.
item.explanation: If wages tracked only acquired skill, the final year should pay like any other; the disproportionate jump at the credential is the anomaly for a pure human-capital story. The signaling option reverses it—the effect supports signaling. The 'more-educated earn more' option is something both theories predict, so it is not what the effect strains. The 'equal amount' option is tempting but mischaracterizes: human capital need not claim equal yearly returns; the tension is the discontinuity at certification, not a claim of equal annual productivity gains.
item.correct_answer: a pure human-capital account in which wages track only the skills acquired through coursework.

distractor_rationales.choice: the signaling account's claim that credentials certify unobservable traits.
the observation that more-educated workers tend to earn higher wages.
the finding that each additional year of schooling raises productivity by an equal amount.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Reyes's conclusion?
choices: Participants' descriptions of how they felt on first hearing the news stayed vivid and emotionally charged throughout the ten-year study.
Some participants' recollections grew more elaborate and detailed with each retelling over the decade.
Participants recalled ordinary events from the same period far less vividly than they recalled the shocking news.
Participants who reported the highest confidence in their recollections also showed the fewest factual distortions over the decade.
item.passage: The confidence people feel in their memories of shocking public events—where they were when they heard the news—has long been taken as a mark of those memories' accuracy. Reyes challenges the equation. In her longitudinal study, participants' recollections drifted substantially over a decade, acquiring false details and shedding true ones, even as their subjective certainty held perfectly steady or rose. Vividness and confidence, she concludes, track not the fidelity of a memory but the emotional force of the original event; a recollection can feel indelible precisely while it is being quietly rewritten. The finding is unsettling because it severs the intuitive link between how sure we feel and how right we are—two quantities that, for these memories, appear to vary independently.
item.explanation: Reyes concludes that confidence and accuracy vary independently. The finding that participants 'who reported the highest confidence in their recollections also showed the fewest factual distortions' restores exactly the link she severs, so it is the direct weakener. The finding that participants' accounts of 'how they felt on first hearing the news' stayed vivid and charged fits her claim that vividness tracks emotional force, and says nothing about accuracy. The finding that some recollections 'grew more elaborate and detailed with each retelling' supports her reconstruction thesis rather than undermining it. And the finding that participants recalled ordinary events 'far less vividly than they recalled the shocking news' compares categories of event, leaving the confidence-accuracy relationship untouched.
item.correct_answer: Participants who reported the highest confidence in their recollections also showed the fewest factual distortions over the decade.

distractor_rationales.choice: Participants' emotional descriptions of the original event remained vivid throughout the ten-year study.
Some participants' recollections grew more elaborate and detailed as the years passed.
Participants recalled ordinary events from the same period far less vividly than the shocking event.

item.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It disputes the well-established claim that volcanic eruptions cool the planet at all, showing that the aerosols they inject in fact warm it.
It grants a well-established short-term effect, then argues that a longer timescale reverses the conclusion one might draw from it.
It weighs two competing cooling mechanisms, sulfate aerosols and carbon dioxide, in order to determine which one more effectively offsets warming.
It uses the example of volcanism to argue that natural sources of climate variability outweigh human influence.
item.passage: That volcanic eruptions can cool the planet is beyond dispute; the sulfate aerosols they inject into the stratosphere reflect sunlight and have measurably lowered global temperatures for a year or two after major eruptions. It is tempting to extrapolate from this to a natural thermostat capable of offsetting warming over the long term. The extrapolation fails on a question of timescale. Aerosols wash out of the stratosphere within a few years, whereas the carbon dioxide that eruptions also release lingers for centuries. Volcanism's cooling is thus a brief flicker atop a slow, cumulative warming; averaged over geological time, volcanoes have almost certainly added net heat, not subtracted it. The very mechanism invoked as a counterweight to warming turns out, on the longer accounting that matters, to sit on the same side of the ledger as the problem it was supposed to solve.
item.explanation: The passage concedes a well-established short-term effect - aerosol cooling is 'beyond dispute' - and then shows that on a centuries-long accounting the CO2 eruptions also release makes volcanism net warming, so a longer timescale reverses the conclusion. That is the answer that grants a well-established short-term effect before arguing that a longer timescale reverses it. The answer that the text disputes the well-established claim that volcanic eruptions cool the planet at all misreads the concession: the cooling is granted outright, and only the extrapolation to a long-term thermostat is denied. The answer describing two competing cooling mechanisms, sulfate aerosols and carbon dioxide, misdescribes the content, since CO2 figures here as the warming agent, not a rival coolant. And the answer that natural sources of climate variability outweigh human influence asserts a conclusion the passage never draws and would resist.
item.correct_answer: It grants a well-established short-term effect, then argues that a longer timescale reverses the conclusion one might draw from it.

distractor_rationales.choice: It disputes the well-established claim that volcanic eruptions cool the planet at all, showing that the aerosols they inject in fact warm it.
It weighs two competing cooling mechanisms, sulfate aerosols and carbon dioxide, in order to determine which one more effectively offsets warming.
It uses the example of volcanism to argue that natural sources of climate variability outweigh human influence.

item.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence?
choices: It concedes that Mercator did after all design his projection to swell the northern continents at the expense of the southern ones, as critics charge.
It proposes that the projection be retired from classrooms and boardrooms in favor of one that renders the relative areas of the continents accurately.
It crystallizes the passage's reframing by separating what the projection represents accurately from the error of using it for the wrong purpose.
It restates the mathematical link between lines of constant compass bearing and areal distortion that the passage has already shown to be inseparable.
item.passage: Critics of the Mercator projection charge that it distorts the world for ideological ends, swelling Europe and North America while shrinking Africa and South America. The distortion is real: Greenland appears as large as Africa, though Africa is roughly fourteen times its area. But the standard critique mistakes the cause. Mercator did not inflate the north to demean the south; he was solving a navigational problem. His projection renders lines of constant compass bearing as straight lines, an indispensable aid to sixteenth-century sailors, and that property is mathematically inseparable from the areal distortion critics decry—you cannot have the one without the other. The map's politics, such as they are, lie not in Mercator's design but in its later use: its persistence in classrooms and boardrooms long after navigation ceased to require it. The projection is not a lie about size; it is a truth about direction, misapplied.
item.explanation: The final sentence - "The projection is not a lie about size; it is a truth about direction, misapplied" - packs the passage's reframing into a single line, separating what the map genuinely represents (constant compass bearings as straight lines) from the error of keeping it in use long after navigation stopped requiring it. That distillation is the function the key names. The option that the sentence "concedes that Mercator did after all design his projection to swell the northern continents" contradicts the passage, which denies any such intent and traces the distortion to the mathematics of the projection. The option that it "proposes that the projection be retired from classrooms and boardrooms" adds a recommendation the passage never issues; it locates the politics in later use without prescribing a replacement. And the option that it merely "restates the mathematical link between lines of constant compass bearing and areal distortion" undersells the sentence, which delivers the interpretive verdict rather than repeating geometry already established.
item.correct_answer: It crystallizes the passage's reframing by separating what the projection represents accurately from the error of using it for the wrong purpose.

distractor_rationales.choice: It concedes that Mercator did after all design his projection to swell the northern continents at the expense of the southern ones, as critics charge.
It proposes that the projection be retired from classrooms and boardrooms in favor of one that renders the relative areas of the continents accurately.
It restates the mathematical link between lines of constant compass bearing and areal distortion that the passage has already shown to be inseparable.

item.prompt: Based on the texts, the historians described in Text 2 would most likely characterize Kuhn's account of paradigm change as
choices: mistaken in claiming that science advances by the steady accumulation of evidence.
overstating the abruptness of a transition that, examined closely, unfolded gradually.
correct about incommensurability but wrong to describe the change as a conversion.
persuasive in its reasoning but unsupported by any evidence from actual historical episodes.
item.passage:
Text 1

Thomas Kuhn transformed the history of science by arguing that it does not advance by steady accumulation. Normal science, he held, proceeds within an unquestioned framework, or paradigm, until anomalies accumulate to the point of crisis; a revolution then installs a new paradigm incommensurable with the old. Because rival paradigms define their terms differently, Kuhn maintained, the change resembles a gestalt switch more than a reasoned tally of evidence—a conversion a community undergoes rather than a sum it computes.

Text 2

Historians since Kuhn have questioned how sharp these breaks really were. Reexamining episodes Kuhn treated as ruptures, they find protracted periods in which old and new frameworks coexisted, practitioners borrowed freely across the supposed divide, and 'incommensurable' vocabularies proved mutually translatable in practice. What looked like a sudden gestalt switch, viewed closely, dissolves into a gradual, negotiated shift with no clean before and after. The revolutionary structure, on this view, is partly an artifact of hindsight, which compresses decades of messy transition into a single decisive turn.
item.explanation: Text 2's historians reexamine the episodes Kuhn treated as ruptures and find "a gradual, negotiated shift with no clean before and after," so what they fault in him is the suddenness - the key's charge of overstating the abruptness of a transition. The option calling Kuhn "mistaken in claiming that science advances by the steady accumulation" of evidence pins on him the exact view Text 1 says he rejected, so it misfires as a criticism of his account. The option that he is "correct about incommensurability but wrong" to describe the change as a conversion concedes the wrong half: Text 2 attacks incommensurability head-on, reporting that those vocabularies "proved mutually translatable in practice." And the option calling him "persuasive in its reasoning but unsupported by any evidence" from actual historical episodes cannot describe these historians, whose entire method is reexamining episodes; their quarrel is with what the episodes show, not with an absence of them.
item.correct_answer: overstating the abruptness of a transition that, examined closely, unfolded gradually.

distractor_rationales.choice: mistaken in claiming that science advances by the steady accumulation of evidence.
correct about incommensurability but wrong to describe the change as a conversion.
persuasive in its reasoning but unsupported by any evidence from actual historical episodes.

item.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Ice-core records demonstrate that changes in carbon dioxide concentration could not have influenced past global temperatures.
Although carbon dioxide did not initiate the last deglaciation, it was essential to the full magnitude of the resulting global warming.
High-resolution dating of ice cores has become precise enough to distinguish events separated by only a few centuries.
Orbital shifts, rather than carbon dioxide, account for both the onset and the eventual magnitude of the last deglaciation.
item.passage: Ice-core records from the last deglaciation are often cited as proof that carbon dioxide drives global temperature. Yet the same cores complicate that story. In Antarctica, temperature and CO2 rose in near lockstep, but high-resolution dating reveals that Antarctic warming began several centuries before CO2 concentrations climbed. Rather than igniting the warming, the gas appears to have entered the atmosphere only after orbital shifts had already nudged the Southern Ocean to release it. This sequence does not diminish carbon dioxide's role; it reframes it. Once liberated, the gas trapped additional heat, and the global average temperature—unlike Antarctica's—did track CO2 closely, rising in step with it across both hemispheres. The initial trigger was astronomical, but the magnitude of the eventual worldwide warming cannot be explained by orbital forcing alone. Carbon dioxide, in this account, is less a spark than an accelerant: incapable of starting the fire on its own, yet indispensable to how far it ultimately spread.
item.explanation: The passage concedes the lag, since Antarctic warming began centuries before CO2 rose and orbital shifts were the trigger, but insists this 'does not diminish' the gas's role and 'reframes it' as an accelerant indispensable to how far the warming spread. Not the spark, essential to the size: that is the main idea. The claim that orbital shifts 'account for both the onset and the eventual magnitude of the last deglaciation' is the tempting overextension, treating the lag as license to explain everything by orbit, when the passage says plainly that the magnitude cannot be explained by orbital forcing alone. The claim that ice-core records show CO2 'could not have influenced past global temperatures' reverses the thesis, since global temperature 'did track CO2 closely.' And the observation that dating 'has become precise enough to distinguish events separated by only a few centuries' is a true methodological detail that enables the argument rather than being it.
item.correct_answer: Although carbon dioxide did not initiate the last deglaciation, it was essential to the full magnitude of the resulting global warming.

distractor_rationales.choice: Ice-core records demonstrate that changes in carbon dioxide concentration could not have influenced past global temperatures.
High-resolution dating of ice cores has become precise enough to distinguish events separated by only a few centuries.
Orbital shifts, rather than carbon dioxide, account for both the onset and the eventual magnitude of the last deglaciation.

item.prompt: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the passage?

It complicates a conservation principle by arguing that a species' origin is a poor proxy for its actual ecological effect.

item.passage: Conservation orthodoxy treats introduced species as threats to be removed. A contrarian argument now circulating does not urge us to welcome invasions, but it does complicate the reflex. In some degraded habitats, the argument notes, a non-native plant may be the only species still stabilizing eroding soil or feeding pollinators whose native food plants have vanished; eradicating it can accelerate the very collapse it was blamed for. The argument stops well short of endorsing introductions. Its narrower point is that 'native' and 'beneficial' are not synonyms, and that a species' origin is a poor substitute for an assessment of what it actually does in a particular, already-altered place.
item.explanation: The passage's stated point is that 'native' and 'beneficial' are not synonyms and that origin is a poor substitute for assessing what a species actually does in a particular altered place. That is the answer that it complicates a conservation principle by arguing that a species' origin is a poor proxy for its actual ecological effect. The answer that it advocates deliberately introducing non-native species into degraded habitats is the tempting overread; the passage twice disclaims it, saying the argument 'does not urge us to welcome invasions' and 'stops well short of endorsing introductions.' The answer that native species are, as a general rule, less beneficial to an altered habitat than the non-native species being removed flips the reflex into an opposite blanket rule, when the claim is that origin alone is uninformative either way. And the answer that defends the orthodox practice of removing every introduced species states the position being complicated, not the passage's purpose.
item.correct_answer: It complicates a conservation principle by arguing that a species' origin is a poor proxy for its actual ecological effect.

distractor_rationales.choice: It advocates deliberately introducing non-native species into degraded habitats where the native plants that once held the soil have vanished.
It contends that native species are, as a general rule, less beneficial to an altered habitat than the non-native species being removed.
It defends the orthodox practice of removing every introduced species, on the ground that a non-native plant is a threat wherever it takes hold.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the passage's reinterpretation of the marshmallow test?
choices: Children from unstable households were less likely to wait for the second marshmallow.
Children who waited longer reported enjoying marshmallows less than those who did not.
The original study drew its participants from a single university community, limiting how broadly its findings about waiting could be generalized.
Children who waited longer still succeeded more as adults even after family background and environmental reliability were fully controlled for.
item.passage: The marshmallow test became a parable of character: children who resisted a treat for a larger later reward grew into more successful adults, proving that self-control is destiny. A reconsideration complicates the moral. When researchers accounted for the children's family circumstances, much of the association between waiting and later success shrank. A child who has learned that promised rewards seldom materialize behaves rationally in grabbing the sure thing; the 'failure' of self-control may instead reflect an accurate read of an unreliable environment. On this account, the test measures not a fixed trait of willpower but a calibrated expectation about whether adults keep their word. What looked like a window onto character may be, in part, a window onto circumstance.
item.explanation: The reinterpretation says the waiting-success link is largely an artifact of circumstance. If the link persists after fully controlling for background and environmental reliability, the circumstance explanation fails and a trait account is restored. The 'unstable households' option supports the reinterpretation. The 'single university community' option (a methodological limit on generalizability) is the tempting trap but does not address the trait-versus-circumstance mechanism, and the 'enjoyed less' option is irrelevant to later success.
item.correct_answer: Children who waited longer still succeeded more as adults even after family background and environmental reliability were fully controlled for.

distractor_rationales.choice: Children from unstable households were less likely to wait for the second marshmallow.
Children who waited longer reported enjoying marshmallows less than those who did not.
The original study drew its participants from a single university community.

item.prompt: Which choice best captures the 'subtler revision' the passage proposes?
choices: Agriculture and monument-building arose at the same time but developed independently of each other.
The site's builders had already domesticated wild cereals before they raised the enclosures.
Monument-building may have been among the causes of agriculture rather than a result of it.
The unusual density of the region's wild cereals made monument-building unnecessary for the site's builders.
item.passage: The monumental stone enclosures at Gobekli Tepe, built by people who left no evidence of farming, have been read as overturning a cornerstone of prehistory: the assumption that agriculture came first and made large-scale construction possible. If foragers could raise multi-ton pillars, the argument goes, then surplus grain was not the precondition for monumental society. Yet the site may warrant a subtler revision rather than a reversal. Excavators note that the region's wild cereals are unusually dense and that the enclosures show signs of periodic, seasonal use rather than permanent settlement. It is possible that the labor of building—and of feeding the builders—created pressures that favored the domestication of those cereals, so that monument-building was not the consequence of agriculture but among its causes.
item.explanation: The 'subtler revision' is that the labor of building the enclosures, and of feeding the builders, may have created pressures favoring domestication of the region's unusually dense wild cereals - so monument-building may have been among the causes of agriculture rather than a result of it. The answer that agriculture and monument-building arose at the same time but developed independently of each other drops exactly the causal link the passage proposes. The answer that the site's builders had already domesticated wild cereals before they raised the enclosures contradicts the stated absence of farming evidence and reverses the proposed order. And the answer that the unusual density of the region's wild cereals made monument-building unnecessary draws a connection the passage never makes; the cereals' abundance is what made their domestication a plausible response to the builders' demands, not a substitute for building.
item.correct_answer: Monument-building may have been among the causes of agriculture rather than a result of it.

distractor_rationales.choice: Agriculture and monument-building arose at the same time but developed independently of each other.
The site's builders had already domesticated wild cereals before they raised the enclosures.
The unusual density of the region's wild cereals made monument-building unnecessary for the site's builders.

item.prompt: Which statement about expert intuition is best supported by the passage?
choices: Expert intuition is a genuine leap past reasoning, arriving at the right move without the slow analysis that a novice has to perform.
Expert intuition reflects compressed prior analysis and is dependable only where patterns recur and feedback is clear.
Because it draws on thousands of stored positions, expert intuition is more accurate than deliberate analysis in nearly every domain, including long-range prediction.
Experts should distrust their intuitions in every field, since the fluency of a judgment never says anything about whether it is likely to be right.
item.passage: The ability of experts to make rapid, accurate judgments is often celebrated as intuition transcending analysis. Chess masters glance at a board and "see" the best move; the feat looks like a leap past reasoning. But studies of expert intuition suggest it is less a departure from analysis than its compression. The master's glance draws on tens of thousands of previously analyzed positions, stored as patterns; what feels immediate is the retrieval of prior, effortful reasoning made automatic through practice. Intuition of this kind is reliable only in domains that are regular enough for patterns to recur and provide feedback clear enough to correct them. Where those conditions fail—as in many long-range predictions—the same confident, effortless judgments become systematically untrustworthy, and their very fluency disguises their unreliability.
item.explanation: The passage defines expert intuition as 'less a departure from analysis than its compression' and makes its reliability conditional on domains regular enough for patterns to recur with feedback clear enough to correct them, which is both halves of the answer. Calling it 'a genuine leap past reasoning, arriving at the right move without the slow analysis' is the celebrated view the passage overturns; what feels immediate is retrieved prior effortful reasoning. Saying it is 'more accurate than deliberate analysis in nearly every domain, including long-range prediction' contradicts the domain-dependence the passage stresses, since long-range prediction is its example of where intuition fails. And urging that experts 'should distrust their intuitions in every field' swings too far the other way: the passage says fluency disguises unreliability where the conditions fail, not that intuition is worthless where they hold.
item.correct_answer: Expert intuition reflects compressed prior analysis and is dependable only where patterns recur and feedback is clear.

distractor_rationales.choice: Expert intuition is a genuine leap past reasoning, arriving at the right move without the slow analysis that a novice has to perform.
Because it draws on thousands of stored positions, expert intuition is more accurate than deliberate analysis in nearly every domain, including long-range prediction.
Experts should distrust their intuitions in every field, since the fluency of a judgment never says anything about whether it is likely to be right.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the researchers' proposed explanation for the gene's rise?
choices: Animal bones show that dairy herds were kept in a region for thousands of years before lactase persistence became common there.
In regions and periods marked by severe famine and epidemic outbreaks, lactase persistence increased in frequency far faster than in stable, well-nourished populations of the same era.
Fermented dairy products such as cheese and yogurt contain far less lactose than fresh milk and cause fewer digestive symptoms.
Modern populations with high rates of lactase persistence drink far more fresh milk per person each year than populations in which the trait remains rare, national consumption figures show.
item.passage: The spread of dairying across ancient Europe is often explained by the evolution of lactase persistence—the ability to digest milk sugar into adulthood. Yet ancient DNA reveals a puzzle: populations kept dairy herds and consumed milk products for millennia before the lactase-persistence gene became common. Some researchers now argue that the gene's later rise was driven not by dairying as a steady food source but by episodes of famine and disease, when the diarrheal cost of drinking unfermented milk turned lethal and any digestive advantage became a matter of survival. On this account, milk consumption did not select for the gene during ordinary times; only under acute stress did the difference between digesting and not digesting milk translate into differential survival.
item.explanation: The proposed explanation is that selection acted only under acute stress, when the diarrheal cost of drinking unfermented milk turned lethal. The finding that in regions and periods 'marked by severe famine and epidemic outbreaks' lactase persistence 'increased in frequency far faster than in stable, well-nourished populations of the same era' is that hypothesis's signature prediction, with the contemporaneous stable populations serving as the control. The finding that 'dairy herds were kept in a region for thousands of years before lactase persistence became common' restates the puzzle the hypothesis was invented to solve rather than testing its mechanism. The fact that 'fermented dairy products such as cheese and yogurt contain far less lactose' explains how milk was tolerable before the gene spread but says nothing about famine-driven selection. And the observation that modern high-persistence populations 'drink far more fresh milk per person each year' points the causal arrow the other way, treating the gene as a cause of present-day consumption rather than testing what drove its rise.
item.correct_answer: In regions and periods marked by severe famine and epidemic outbreaks, lactase persistence increased in frequency far faster than in stable, well-nourished populations of the same era.

distractor_rationales.choice: Animal bones show that dairy herds were kept in a region for thousands of years before lactase persistence became common there.
Fermented dairy products such as cheese and yogurt contain far less lactose than fresh milk and cause fewer digestive symptoms.
Modern populations with high rates of lactase persistence drink far more fresh milk per person each year than populations in which the trait remains rare, national consumption figures show.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's central claim?
choices: A neighboring state that imported identical Western machinery but lacked comparable commercial institutions failed to industrialize at a similar pace.
The Meiji government spent more on foreign machinery than any other contemporaneous Asian state.
Foreign advisers in Japan were paid substantially higher salaries than they had earned at home, a premium that drew engineers and accountants to Meiji ministries.
Tokugawa-era literacy rates were significantly lower in rural regions than in major cities.
item.passage: Standard narratives attribute Japan's swift industrialization after 1868 to the Meiji government's importation of Western machinery and foreign advisers. The hardware mattered, but it does not explain why Japan absorbed what other nineteenth-century states could not. Long before Commodore Perry, Tokugawa Japan possessed high literacy, a dense commercial network, sophisticated rural proto-industry, and merchant houses skilled in double-entry accounting and futures trading. These endowments meant that imported technology met a workforce and a managerial class already primed to deploy it. Foreign experts were, tellingly, dismissed as soon as Japanese personnel could replace them—often within a decade. The Meiji reformers' genuine innovation lay less in acquiring foreign techniques than in redirecting indigenous capacities toward national ends. Where historians once read the period as a story of borrowing, the more defensible reading treats borrowing as the visible surface of a deeper continuity, one that the drama of Westernization has tended to obscure.
item.explanation: The thesis is that Japan absorbed Western technology because of indigenous endowments - high literacy, dense commercial networks, rural proto-industry, merchant houses skilled in accounting - rather than because of the imports themselves. A neighboring state that "imported identical Western machinery but lacked comparable commercial institutions" and still failed to industrialize holds the hardware constant while varying the institutions, isolating them as the decisive factor. The option that the Meiji government "spent more on foreign machinery than any other" contemporaneous Asian state measures the borrowing the author is demoting and says nothing about domestic capacity. The detail that advisers "were paid substantially higher salaries" than at home is true but idle here; what matters to the argument is how fast they were dismissed, not what they cost. And the finding that "literacy rates were significantly lower in rural regions" would chip away at the sophisticated rural proto-industry the author leans on, weakening the claim rather than strengthening it.
item.correct_answer: A neighboring state that imported identical Western machinery but lacked comparable commercial institutions failed to industrialize at a similar pace.

distractor_rationales.choice: The Meiji government spent more on foreign machinery than any other contemporaneous Asian state.
Foreign advisers in Japan were paid substantially higher salaries than they had earned at home.
Tokugawa-era literacy rates were significantly lower in rural regions than in major cities.

item.prompt: The author would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Unreliable narration shows that no determinate truth underlies a story, only a set of competing perspectives.
Readers cannot distinguish a reliable narrator from an unreliable one without evidence from outside the text.
Unreliable narration is a distinctively modern technique that earlier writers of fiction avoided.
Recognizing a narrator as unreliable depends on the reader's assumption that a determinate truth exists.
item.passage: Critics often treat the unreliable narrator as fiction's great solvent of certainty, a device that dissolves any stable truth into competing perspectives. The device does the opposite. For a narrator to register as unreliable, the reader must detect the gap between what is said and what is the case—must, that is, reconstruct the very facts the narrator distorts. A story narrated by a liar is legible only because the reader triangulates toward a truth the liar conceals; unreliability is a technique for pointing at reality by the roundabout route of misdescribing it. Far from abandoning the notion of a determinate world, such fiction depends on the reader's confidence that one exists and can be inferred. The narrator who cannot be trusted thus presupposes a reader who trusts that trustworthiness is possible. What looks like radical skepticism is, on inspection, a covert affirmation of the standards it appears to flout.
item.explanation: The author argues that to register a narrator as unreliable the reader must 'reconstruct the very facts the narrator distorts,' so the device 'depends on the reader's confidence' that a determinate world exists, which is precisely the answer. The statement that unreliable narration 'shows that no determinate truth underlies a story, only a set of competing perspectives' is the critics' view the passage cites and then reverses with 'The device does the opposite.' The claim that 'readers cannot distinguish a reliable narrator from an unreliable one without evidence from outside the text' introduces an external-evidence requirement the passage never makes; on its account the reader triangulates from within the story. And calling unreliable narration 'a distinctively modern technique that earlier writers of fiction avoided' is a historical assertion with no basis in the text, which never dates the device.
item.correct_answer: Recognizing a narrator as unreliable depends on the reader's assumption that a determinate truth exists.

distractor_rationales.choice: Unreliable narration shows that no determinate truth underlies a story, only a set of competing perspectives.
Readers cannot distinguish a reliable narrator from an unreliable one without evidence from outside the text.
Unreliable narration is a distinctively modern technique that earlier writers of fiction avoided.

item.prompt: Which choice is most strongly supported by the text?
choices: Elder trees deliberately route sugars through the fungal network to their own shaded seedlings in order to improve those seedlings' survival.
The transfer of carbon between trees may be better explained by the fungi's self-interest than by cooperation among the trees themselves.
The fungi that form these underground bridges ferry carbon to shaded seedlings at a net metabolic loss to themselves, taking no toll in return.
The fungal networks connecting tree root systems have been shown not to transfer carbon between them at all.
item.passage: Popular accounts celebrate the 'wood-wide web,' the underground fungal filaments that link trees and, reportedly, allow elder trees to nurse seedlings with shared sugars. That carbon moves between root systems is well documented. But the inference of deliberate benevolence rests on a slender foundation. The fungi that form these bridges are not passive cables; they are organisms with their own metabolic interests, and they extract a substantial toll from every sugar molecule they ferry. Carbon may flow toward a shaded seedling not because a donor tree 'chooses' to give, but because the fungal partner routes resources wherever they secure the fungus its own future. What looks like arboreal charity may be, at bottom, fungal husbandry. The network is real; the generosity attributed to trees is an interpretation the evidence does not compel.
item.explanation: The passage keeps the phenomenon and challenges its interpretation: carbon does move between root systems, but it may move because the fungal partner 'routes resources wherever they secure the fungus its own future,' making the flow 'fungal husbandry' rather than 'arboreal charity.' That is the fungal self-interest reading. The option saying that 'elder trees deliberately route sugars through the fungal network to their own shaded seedlings' is the popular benevolence narrative the text calls an interpretation the evidence does not compel. The option saying the fungi 'ferry carbon to shaded seedlings at a net metabolic loss to themselves, taking no toll in return' reverses the passage's key fact, that they 'extract a substantial toll from every sugar molecule they ferry.' And the option saying the networks 'have been shown not to transfer carbon between them at all' contradicts the concession the whole argument is built on, that carbon movement between root systems 'is well documented.'
item.correct_answer: The transfer of carbon between trees may be better explained by the fungi's self-interest than by cooperation among the trees themselves.

distractor_rationales.choice: Elder trees deliberately route sugars through the fungal network to their own shaded seedlings in order to improve those seedlings' survival.
The fungi that form these underground bridges ferry carbon to shaded seedlings at a net metabolic loss to themselves, taking no toll in return.
The fungal networks connecting tree root systems have been shown not to transfer carbon between them at all.

item.prompt: Based on the two texts, the authors would most likely disagree about whether
choices: Antarctic temperature began rising several centuries before atmospheric CO2 did at the end of past ice ages
cyclical shifts in Earth's orbit contributed to triggering the onset of past deglaciations in the southern ocean
atmospheric carbon dioxide is physically capable of trapping heat in the atmosphere at all
the several-century lag shows that CO2 played only a minor role in the warming that followed
item.passage:
Text 1: Ice cores drilled from Antarctica record that, at the end of past ice ages, Antarctic temperature began rising several centuries before atmospheric carbon dioxide did. To some, this lag is decisive: if warming preceded the rise in CO2, then CO2 cannot have driven the warming, and its role in climate has been overstated.

Text 2: The Antarctic lead is genuine, but the inference drawn from it is not. Deglaciations were triggered by cyclical shifts in Earth's orbit that warmed the southern ocean first; that initial warming then released CO2, which trapped heat and drove the far larger, globally synchronized warming that followed. Carbon dioxide acted here as an amplifier rather than an initial trigger—a role the lag does nothing to diminish. A spark may precede a fire without the fuel being incidental to the blaze.
item.explanation: Text 1 treats the lag as decisive proof that CO2's role has been 'overstated'; Text 2 replies that 'the inference drawn from it is not' sound and casts CO2 as the amplifier of the far larger warming that followed. So the disagreement is over whether the several-century lag shows that CO2 played only a minor role in the warming that followed. That Antarctic temperature began rising several centuries before atmospheric CO2 did is common ground - Text 2 calls the lead 'genuine' - so it is agreed, not disputed. That cyclical shifts in Earth's orbit contributed to triggering the onset of past deglaciations is asserted only by Text 2 and nowhere contested by Text 1, which offers no rival trigger. And whether carbon dioxide is physically capable of trapping heat at all is affirmed by Text 2 and never denied by Text 1, whose quarrel is with the size of CO2's role, not its physics.
item.correct_answer: the several-century lag shows that CO2 played only a minor role in the warming that followed

distractor_rationales.choice: Antarctic temperature began rising several centuries before atmospheric CO2 did at the end of past ice ages
cyclical shifts in Earth's orbit contributed to triggering the onset of past deglaciations in the southern ocean

item.prompt: Which statement is most strongly supported by the text?
choices: Much of the happiness gap between volunteers and non-volunteers reflects preexisting differences in who volunteers rather than an effect of the volunteering.
Volunteering has no genuine effect at all on a person's well-being once the preexisting differences between the people who volunteer and those who do not are accounted for.

item.passage: Surveys reliably find that people who volunteer report greater happiness than those who do not, a correlation frequently presented as proof that donating one's time lifts one's mood. Longitudinal data invite more caution than the surveys allow. Tracking the same individuals across many years, researchers found that a rise in a person's happiness tended to precede an increase in their volunteering about as often as it followed one—in other words, people who had grown happier for other reasons subsequently took up volunteering. The activity did still produce a genuine well-being benefit, but a distinctly modest one, far smaller than the gap in any single year's snapshot would imply. Most of that headline gap, it turns out, reflects a difference in who chooses to volunteer in the first place rather than any transformation worked by the volunteering itself.
item.explanation: The passage says 'most of that headline gap... reflects a difference in who chooses to volunteer' rather than what volunteering does—selection, not treatment—which is the answer “reflects preexisting differences in who volunteers”. The choice “Volunteering has no genuine effect at all” overstates: the text explicitly grants 'a genuine well-being benefit,' just a modest one, so 'no genuine effect' is wrong (the tempting flattening). The choice “reliably generate large and lasting gains” reverses the finding, which downgrades the effect to 'distinctly modest,' not large. The choice “the group least likely to take up volunteering” reverses the direction: it was 'happier' people, not unhappy ones, who tended to take up volunteering afterward.
item.correct_answer: Much of the happiness gap between volunteers and non-volunteers reflects preexisting differences in who volunteers rather than an effect of the volunteering.
