item.prompt: How does the research described in Text 2 complicate Socrates's warning in Text 1?
choices: It vindicates Socrates completely, showing that people who keep a written record remember less of everything, including where the record itself is kept.
It refutes Socrates by showing that keeping a written record leaves a person’s recall entirely unaffected.
It supports part of Socrates's warning (weaker recall of recorded specifics) while showing that memory is redirected rather than simply diminished.
It demonstrates that people in oral cultures — those without writing — remembered less than literate people who keep written records.
item.passage:
Text 1: In Plato's Phaedrus, Socrates warns that writing will weaken memory: relying on external marks, people will cease to cultivate the disciplined recollection that oral cultures prize. The written word, he suggests, offers only the semblance of wisdom.

Text 2: Modern research on 'cognitive offloading' finds that people who expect to have a written record recall the recorded information itself less well—but recall better where to find it, and free mental resources for other tasks. Offloading does not simply degrade memory; it redistributes what memory is used for.
item.explanation: Text 2 splits Socrates's warning in two. It confirms one half - people who expect a written record "recall the recorded information itself less well" - and then complicates the rest, since those same people recall better where to find it and free mental resources for other tasks. Memory is redistributed rather than simply degraded, which is the key. The option that the research "vindicates Socrates completely," showing that people "remember less of everything, including where the record itself is kept," contradicts the finding about locating information. The option that keeping a record leaves "recall entirely unaffected" ignores the conceded loss of recorded specifics, which Text 2 reports plainly. And the option comparing people in oral cultures with "literate people who keep written records" invokes a comparison Text 2 never runs; its evidence is about what an individual expects to have recorded, not about the memory of whole cultures.
item.correct_answer: It supports part of Socrates's warning (weaker recall of recorded specifics) while showing that memory is redirected rather than simply diminished.

distractor_rationales.choice: It vindicates Socrates completely, showing that people who keep a written record remember less of everything, including where the record itself is kept.
It refutes Socrates by showing that keeping a written record leaves a person’s recall entirely unaffected.
It demonstrates that people in oral cultures — those without writing — remembered less than literate people who keep written records.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen Marchetti's argument?
choices: Elk numbers fell sharply in the years just after the wolves returned to the park.
Beaver colonies have multiplied along several Yellowstone streams in the years since the wolves were returned to the park.
In valleys where wolves are abundant but groundwater is deep, willow cover has continued to decline.
Wolves reintroduced to other national parks have cut local deer numbers within a few seasons.
item.passage: The return of wolves to Yellowstone has become a parable of ecological cascade: predators cull the elk, browsed willows recover, beavers return, and rivers themselves stabilize. Marchetti's data invite caution. Willow regrowth, he finds, tracks not the mere presence of wolves but local water-table depth and the independent decline of elk from drought and from hunting outside the park; in drier reaches where wolves hunt freely, willows have not rebounded at all. The wolves are one influence among several, not the lone lever the parable implies. To credit them with remaking the rivers is to compress a tangle of interacting causes into a single satisfying chain—satisfying precisely because it restores a comforting faith that removing one wrong and adding one right can set a whole system back in order.
item.explanation: Marchetti argues that wolves are one influence among several, not the lone lever. The finding that 'in valleys where wolves are abundant but groundwater is deep, willow cover has continued to decline' isolates his variable: predation is present, hydrology is not, and the recovery fails — so wolves alone are insufficient. The finding that 'elk numbers fell sharply in the years just after' the wolves returned and the finding that 'beaver colonies have multiplied along several Yellowstone streams' both sit comfortably inside the single-chain parable he is questioning, so neither strengthens him. And the finding about wolves in other parks cutting 'local deer numbers within a few seasons' concerns predator-prey dynamics elsewhere, not the willow-and-water mechanism at issue here.
item.correct_answer: In valleys where wolves are abundant but groundwater is deep, willow cover has continued to decline.

distractor_rationales.choice: Elk numbers fell sharply in the years just after the wolves returned to the park.
Beaver colonies have multiplied along several Yellowstone streams in the years since the wolves were returned to the park.
Wolves reintroduced to other national parks have cut local deer numbers within a few seasons.

item.prompt: Based on the texts, how would Davis (Text 2) most likely respond to the "presumption against non-natives" described in Text 1?
choices: He would argue that it misdirects effort by treating a species' foreign origin, rather than its actual effect, as the mark of a threat.
He would reject it outright, denying that introduced predators have driven island endemics to extinction.
He would endorse it as a reasonable default, urging still stricter controls on islands where endemics lack defenses.
He would accept the presumption for introduced predators while insisting that introduced competitors usually enrich the communities they join.
item.passage:
Text 1

Conservation policy has long treated non-native species as threats to be eradicated. The rationale is well grounded: introduced predators and competitors have driven numerous native species to extinction, particularly on islands, where endemic organisms evolved without defenses against the newcomers. Left unchecked, an aggressive invader can restructure an entire community, homogenizing distinctive local biotas into a repetitive global assemblage. For managers charged with preserving native diversity, the presumption against non-natives is a reasonable default.

Text 2

Ecologist Mark Davis argues that the reflex to condemn all non-natives confuses origin with impact. Most introduced species, he observes, neither spread aggressively nor harm their new communities; many integrate quietly, and at regional scales the arrival of non-natives has frequently raised, not lowered, the total number of species present. The relevant question, Davis insists, is not where an organism came from but what it does. Judging a species by its passport rather than its behavior, he warns, squanders scarce conservation effort on harmless immigrants.
item.explanation: Davis's position is that the reflex to condemn all non-natives 'confuses origin with impact,' and that judging a species 'by its passport rather than its behavior' squanders scarce conservation effort, so he would attack the presumption for keying on origin instead of effect. The response that he would 'reject it outright, denying that introduced predators have driven island endemics to extinction' overstates him: he says most introduced species are harmless, which concedes that some are not, and he never disputes the island extinctions Text 1 cites. The response that he would 'endorse it as a reasonable default, urging still stricter controls on islands' reverses his argument, and 'reasonable default' is Text 1's phrase rather than his. And the response that he would 'accept the presumption for introduced predators while insisting that introduced competitors usually enrich the communities they join' invents a predator-versus-competitor split; Davis sorts species by what they do, not by ecological role.
item.correct_answer: He would argue that it misdirects effort by treating a species' foreign origin, rather than its actual effect, as the mark of a threat.

distractor_rationales.choice: He would reject it, maintaining that non-native species do not in fact drive native species to extinction.
He would endorse it as a reasonable default while noting that island ecosystems require even stricter controls.
He would accept it for introduced predators but argue that introduced competitors are usually beneficial.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the carbon-dioxide hypothesis over the water hypothesis?
choices: The Martian gullies closely resemble the channels that seasonal runoff cuts in desert slopes on Earth.
Clay minerals that form only after prolonged exposure to liquid water have been identified in ancient terrain far from the gullies.
Time-lapse imaging shows gully material moving during the coldest months, when CO2 frost is present but liquid water cannot exist.
The gullies sit on slopes steep enough for loose debris to slide under gravity alone, without any lubricant.
item.passage: When narrow gullies were photographed on Martian crater walls, they were quickly read as the fingerprints of flowing water, and thus of a planet perhaps hospitable to life. The channels do resemble those water carves on Earth. But resemblance is not mechanism. Many of the gullies lie in places too cold for liquid water to persist, and their activity peaks not in the Martian summer but in the depths of winter, when carbon-dioxide frost accumulates and then sublimates. A growing number of planetary scientists therefore suspect the sculptor is not water at all but blocks of dry ice, lubricated by the gas they release as they slide. If so, the gullies say little about Mars's habitability.
item.explanation: The carbon-dioxide account depends on the gullies being active in winter, when CO2 frost sublimates and liquid water cannot persist. Time-lapse imaging showing gully material moving during the coldest months is exactly that discriminator: it fits sliding dry ice and excludes flowing water. The finding that the Martian gullies closely resemble the channels that seasonal runoff cuts in desert slopes on Earth is the trap - it leans toward the water reading, and the passage warns that 'resemblance is not mechanism.' The clay minerals that form only after prolonged exposure to liquid water are found in ancient terrain far from the gullies, so they speak to Mars's distant past, not to what carved these channels. And slopes steep enough for loose debris to slide under gravity alone would serve either agent equally, so that finding separates the two hypotheses not at all.
item.correct_answer: Time-lapse imaging shows gully material moving during the coldest months, when CO2 frost is present but liquid water cannot exist.

distractor_rationales.choice: The Martian gullies are shaped very similarly to water-cut channels found in deserts on Earth.
Mineral deposits requiring long exposure to liquid water are found elsewhere on Mars.
The gullies occur on slopes steep enough for loose material to slide under gravity alone.

item.prompt: The author would most likely agree that the Impressionists' break with the Salon
choices: coincided with and took advantage of changes already transforming the art market
was primarily an act of aesthetic principle undertaken in spite of its commercial cost
single-handedly created the modern system of private art dealers
failed commercially because it alienated established collectors
item.passage: The Impressionists are conventionally remembered as embattled radicals, spurned by the official Salon and painting in defiant poverty. There is truth in the image, but it flatters a more calculating reality. Excluded from the state-run Salon, painters like Monet and Degas did not merely suffer their exclusion; they turned to the emerging network of private dealers and independent exhibitions that was reshaping the art market. Dealers such as Paul Durand-Ruel cultivated collectors, staged solo shows, and stabilized prices—functions the Salon had never performed for living artists. The much-mythologized independent exhibitions were, among other things, shrewd commercial ventures that bypassed a gatekeeper the market was already rendering obsolete. To read Impressionism purely as aesthetic insurgency is to miss how neatly its rebellion aligned with, and profited from, a structural shift already underway in how art was sold.
item.explanation: The author reframes the celebrated insurgency as aligning with, and profiting from, 'a structural shift already underway in how art was sold' - the answer that the break coincided with and took advantage of changes already transforming the art market. The answer that it was primarily an act of aesthetic principle undertaken in spite of its commercial cost is the embattled-radical image the passage grants only in order to complicate ('it flatters a more calculating reality'). The answer that the break single-handedly created the modern system of private art dealers reverses the causation: the dealer network was already 'emerging' and was 'already rendering' the Salon obsolete before the painters turned to it. And the answer that it failed commercially because it alienated established collectors contradicts the text, which credits Durand-Ruel with cultivating collectors and stabilizing prices.

item.prompt: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that the author regards the printing press's early effect on the control of ideas as

item.passage: The printing press is routinely credited with democratizing knowledge by making books cheap and abundant. In the long run it did. But in the decades immediately following its spread, its effect on the circulation of ideas was more ambiguous. Printing enormously amplified the output of already-dominant institutions—churches, states, and established universities, which alone could fund large print runs—so that the first great surge of printed matter consisted overwhelmingly of official texts, indulgences, and orthodox commentary. Heterodox works could be printed too, but they could also be identified, catalogued, and suppressed with a new efficiency once they existed in fixed, traceable editions. The press did not immediately loosen authority's grip on the written word; for a time it tightened it, handing the powerful a tool whose leveling potential would be realized only later.
item.explanation: The passage concedes that in the long run the press democratized knowledge but says that for a time it 'tightened' authority's grip, its leveling potential 'realized only later,' which is the two-stage view the answer captures. Describing the effect as 'an immediate and decisive weakening of established authority over the written word' is the popular story the passage postpones rather than endorses. And calling the effect 'negligible, because print runs remained too expensive for any institution to exploit' contradicts the text outright, which says churches, states, and universities alone could fund large print runs, and did.

As notation spread, it did not merely preserve music; it quietly privileged the music it could preserve, nudging composition toward the notatable and casting the unnotatable as imprecision. What we take for music's natural evolution toward complexity was in part an artifact of the tool we used to write it down.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's challenge to Jacobs's argument?
choices: A survey finds that residents across many cities say they strongly prefer to live in neighborhoods that mix shops and homes on the same block.
A study finds that when neighborhoods grew safer for reasons unrelated to development, pedestrian activity rose only afterward.
Cities that have adopted more mixed-use zoning tend to report lower rates of street crime than comparable cities zoned for one use.
Adding streetlights to a poorly lit district was followed by a measurable drop in nighttime crime over the two years that followed.
item.passage: Jane Jacobs's celebrated argument that busy, mixed-use sidewalks deter crime by furnishing 'eyes on the street' has hardened into planning orthodoxy: fill a block with shops and strollers, and safety follows. The correlation is well attested, but its direction is not. Streets teem with pedestrians largely where people already feel safe enough to linger; where they do not, no zoning code conjures a crowd. What Jacobs read as cause may often be effect—the lively sidewalk a symptom of an underlying security rather than its source. This inversion matters for policy, because a city that expects mixed-use development to pacify a dangerous district by itself may be prescribing the fever to cure the disease. None of this refutes the value of active streets, which remain worth cultivating. It cautions only against assuming that the surveillance they provide is doing the causal work their mere presence is so often credited with.
item.explanation: The author's challenge is that Jacobs may have the causal arrow backward: safety draws the crowd rather than the crowd producing safety. The study finding that when neighborhoods 'grew safer for reasons unrelated to development, pedestrian activity rose only afterward' supplies the ordering that settles direction, with safety first and footfall second. The finding that mixed-use cities 'tend to report lower rates of street crime' is the tempting trap, because it merely restates the correlation both sides already accept and is if anything what Jacobs would predict. The survey showing residents 'strongly prefer to live in neighborhoods that mix shops and homes' reports preferences, not causation. And the finding that 'adding streetlights to a poorly lit district' cut crime tests a different intervention entirely and leaves the pedestrian-safety ordering untouched.
item.correct_answer: A study finds that when neighborhoods grew safer for reasons unrelated to development, pedestrian activity rose only afterward.

distractor_rationales.choice: A survey finds that residents across many cities say they strongly prefer to live in neighborhoods that mix shops and homes on the same block.
Cities that have adopted more mixed-use zoning tend to report lower rates of street crime than comparable cities zoned for one use.
Adding streetlights to a poorly lit district was followed by a measurable drop in nighttime crime over the two years that followed.

item.prompt: Which choice best states what can reasonably be inferred from the passage?
choices: A sufficiently skilled translator can carry every overtone of the original across, leaving nothing to be sacrificed
Words for complex feelings, such as 'saudade,' cannot be carried into another language at all
Fidelity to a text's tone always matters more than fidelity to its literal wording
Producing a translation necessarily involves interpretive choices that no fully faithful rendering could avoid
item.passage: A translation is commonly judged by its fidelity, as though the ideal version were a pane of glass through which the original passes undistorted. The metaphor misleads. A word in one language rarely maps onto a single word in another; to render a term like 'saudade' the translator must choose which of its overtones to preserve and which to sacrifice, and no choice preserves them all. Fidelity to the letter can betray the tone; fidelity to the tone can betray the letter. The translator is thus not a transparent medium but an interpreter forced to decide what a text most essentially is—and every such decision forecloses others. To ask for a translation with no interpretation in it is to ask for no translation at all.
item.explanation: The passage argues that because no rendering preserves every overtone, the translator must interpret; a non-interpretive translation is 'no translation at all.' The trap ('complete fidelity') is the glass-pane ideal the passage rejects. 'Cannot be translated at all' overstates a claim about loss, not impossibility, and ranking tone above letter contradicts the passage's presentation of the two as an unavoidable trade-off.
item.correct_answer: Producing a translation necessarily involves interpretive choices that no fully faithful rendering could avoid

distractor_rationales.choice: A sufficiently skilled translator can carry every overtone of the original across, leaving nothing to be sacrificed
Words for complex feelings, such as 'saudade,' cannot be carried into another language at all
Fidelity to a text's tone always matters more than fidelity to its literal wording

item.prompt: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to
choices: deny that warfare contributed in any way to the emergence of centralized states.
warn that an elegant causal story can substitute for proof that the proposed cause actually operated.
demonstrate that commercial wealth, rather than warfare, produced the centralized state.
explain how gunpowder weaponry rendered traditional fortifications obsolete.
item.passage: Historians once explained the rise of the centralized European state with a simple chain: gunpowder made medieval fortifications obsolete, siege warfare grew ruinously expensive, and only rulers who could tax and borrow on a large scale survived—so war built the modern state. The thesis is elegant, and for that reason worth distrusting. Its neat causal sequence assumes what it should demonstrate: that fiscal centralization followed military necessity rather than preceding and enabling it. Several polities built formidable armies without developing centralized bureaucracies, hiring them through contractors and financiers, while some centralizing states faced little external threat. The 'military revolution' may describe a correlation that ran in both directions, or that some third factor—commercial wealth, say—drove independently. To call war the maker of the state is to mistake a plausible story for a demonstrated cause.
item.explanation: The passage flags the thesis as 'elegant, and for that reason worth distrusting' because it 'assumes what it should demonstrate,' concluding one must not 'mistake a plausible story for a demonstrated cause'—the caution in the answer, “an elegant causal story can substitute for proof”. The choice “deny that warfare contributed in any way” overstates: the author disputes war as a demonstrated cause, not any contribution. The choice “commercial wealth, rather than warfare, produced” is only floated as a possibility ('commercial wealth, say'), never established. The choice “gunpowder weaponry rendered traditional fortifications obsolete” describes a recounted premise of the old thesis, not the author's own purpose.
item.correct_answer: warn that an elegant causal story can substitute for proof that the proposed cause actually operated.

distractor_rationales.choice: deny that warfare contributed in any way to the emergence of centralized states.
demonstrate that commercial wealth, rather than warfare, produced the centralized state.
explain how gunpowder weaponry rendered traditional fortifications obsolete.

item.prompt: Which choice best states what can reasonably be inferred about the examination reform?

It largely preserved the existing distribution of privilege while changing how that privilege was justified
Its classical examinations were deliberately designed to test the skills that office actually required
item.passage: The nineteenth-century campaign to replace patronage appointments with competitive examinations is remembered as a democratizing reform, opening government office to talent rather than connections. Its immediate effect was more equivocal. Because the examinations tested precisely the classical curriculum available only at elite schools, they did not so much dismantle privilege as launder it, converting inherited advantage into the appearance of earned merit. A gatekeeping once nakedly political became procedurally neutral in form while remaining, in its results, remarkably continuous with what it replaced. The reform's lasting achievement was thus less the redistribution of opportunity than the relocation of its justification—from birth to a 'merit' that birth still largely determined.
item.explanation: The passage says the reform 'laundered' privilege—neutral in form, 'remarkably continuous' in results—relocating its justification from birth to a birth-determined 'merit.' The trap ('rapidly opened... every background') is the celebratory reading the passage qualifies. 'Less fair than patronage' overstates 'remarkably continuous' (not worse), and 'designed to measure administrative competence' contradicts the point that it tested classics tied to elite schooling.
item.correct_answer: It largely preserved the existing distribution of privilege while changing how that privilege was justified

distractor_rationales.choice: It rapidly opened government positions to talented candidates from every social background, ending the hold of patronage on appointments
It was, in practice, a less fair method of selection than the patronage system it replaced, since it hid privilege that had been visible

item.prompt: The main purpose of the passage is to
choices: determine which physical feature accounts for the old violins' superior tone.
establish that modern violins sound better than old Italian instruments.
call into doubt whether the superiority that decades of research have tried to explain is real.
explain why double-blind testing has become the standard method in acoustics research.
item.passage: The tonal supremacy of a Stradivarius violin is treated almost as a law of nature, and generations of researchers have hunted for its physical cause—in the density of Alpine wood, in a chemical varnish, in the little ice age's slow-grown trees. The search presumes what recent experiments call into question. In double-blind trials, accomplished soloists, unable to see the instruments they played, have repeatedly failed to distinguish celebrated old Italian violins from fine modern ones, and have often preferred the new. If expert listeners and players cannot reliably tell the difference, then the 'secret' of the old instruments' superior sound may be a secret with nothing to explain—an artifact of reputation, price, and the knowledge of what one is holding. The centuries of acoustic sleuthing may have been answering a question that begins by assuming its own conclusion.
item.explanation: The passage says the hunt for a physical cause 'presumes what recent experiments call into question' and raises the possibility of 'a secret with nothing to explain,' so its purpose is to doubt the premise rather than solve the puzzle. Setting out to 'determine which physical feature accounts for the old violins' superior tone' assumes the very superiority the passage suspects is an artifact of reputation and price. Setting out to 'establish that modern violins sound better than old Italian instruments' overreads the evidence: soloists could not tell the instruments apart and 'often preferred the new,' which shows indistinguishability plus a mild preference, not demonstrated superiority. And explaining 'why double-blind testing has become the standard method in acoustics research' mistakes the passage's instrument for its subject, since the blind trials are cited as evidence and never examined as a methodological development.
item.correct_answer: call into doubt whether the superiority that decades of research have tried to explain is real.

distractor_rationales.choice: determine which physical feature accounts for the old violins' superior tone.
establish that modern violins sound better than old Italian instruments.
explain why double-blind testing has become the standard method in acoustics research.

item.prompt: Which choice best states the inference the passage most strongly supports?
choices: Copernicus's model displaced Ptolemy's chiefly because it predicted planetary motions more accurately

A theory that is ultimately correct may, when first proposed, lack a decisive empirical advantage over its rivals

item.passage: The triumph of Copernican astronomy is often narrated as reason vanquishing dogma—a simpler, more accurate model displacing a convoluted one. The early history resists the story. Copernicus, committed like his predecessors to perfectly circular orbits, still required epicycles to fit the observations; his system was not appreciably simpler than Ptolemy's, nor did it predict planetary positions more accurately. Its initial appeal was largely aesthetic and cosmological, not empirical. Only decades later, when Kepler abandoned the circle for the ellipse, did heliocentrism gain a decisive predictive edge. The lesson is not that evidence is dispensable but that a theory can be broadly right for reasons the evidence of its own day does not yet supply.
item.explanation: The passage shows early heliocentrism was no simpler or more accurate than Ptolemy's, gaining its edge only later with Kepler—so a right theory can begin without empirical superiority. The trap restates the standard narrative the passage rejects. 'Evidence played no role' overstates a passage that insists 'evidence is not dispensable,' and the Kepler option reverses the text, which credits ellipses with the decisive edge.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Ogilvie's argument?
choices: Surviving guild ordinances contain detailed technical specifications for acceptable workmanship.
Consumers in guild-controlled towns reported higher satisfaction with the goods they purchased.
Guild apprenticeships typically lasted seven years, longer than the training required in most unregulated trades.
In towns where guilds lost their legal monopolies, the average quality of craft goods remained unchanged while prices fell.
item.passage: Medieval craft guilds are often praised as guarantors of quality: by setting standards and training apprentices, they supposedly protected consumers from shoddy work. The historian Sheilagh Ogilvie contends this benign portrait inverts the evidence. Guild ordinances, she notes, devoted far more text to restricting who could practice a trade—excluding women, migrants, and rural competitors—than to defining what counted as good work. Where quality rules existed, they were enforced selectively, chiefly against outsiders. The guild's core achievement, on this account, was not the protection of buyers but the capture of monopoly profits for a closed circle of masters. Quality was less the guilds' purpose than their pretext.
item.explanation: Ogilvie's claim is that guilds captured monopoly profits and used quality as a pretext. The finding that in towns where guilds lost their monopolies 'the average quality of craft goods remained unchanged while prices fell' separates the two hypotheses cleanly: remove the monopoly and only price moves, so the monopoly was doing price work, not quality work. The finding that ordinances 'contain detailed technical specifications for acceptable workmanship' and the finding that consumers 'reported higher satisfaction with the goods they purchased' both support the benign portrait Ogilvie is attacking, and are the intuitive traps. The finding that apprenticeships 'typically lasted seven years' is true-but-inconclusive: long training could serve quality or serve entry restriction, so it fails to distinguish her account from the one she rejects.
item.correct_answer: In towns where guilds lost their legal monopolies, the average quality of craft goods remained unchanged while prices fell.

distractor_rationales.choice: Surviving guild ordinances contain detailed technical specifications for acceptable workmanship.
Consumers in guild-controlled towns reported higher satisfaction with the goods they purchased.
Guild apprenticeships typically lasted seven years, longer than the training required in most unregulated trades.

item.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the question "Why, then, did agriculture spread?" in the text?
choices: It introduces the author's concession that agriculture ultimately did improve human health despite early setbacks.
It signals that the author will now set aside the skeletal evidence just presented, treating comparisons of farmers with foragers as inconclusive.
It marks a turn from evidence that farming harmed individuals to an explanation of its spread that does not depend on individual benefit.
It invites readers to consider foraging societies as a model preferable to modern agriculture.
item.passage: The transition to agriculture is conventionally cast as humanity's decisive step upward—the innovation that freed our ancestors from the precariousness of foraging. Skeletal evidence unsettles the story. Early farming populations, compared with the foragers who preceded them, were shorter, showed more signs of nutritional stress, and carried a heavier load of infectious disease, the predictable result of denser settlement and a narrower diet. Why, then, did agriculture spread? Not because it made individuals healthier but because it made populations larger: a field feeds more people per acre than a forest, even if it feeds each of them worse. Agriculture triumphed as a demographic strategy, not a nutritional one. The measure by which we call it progress—the sheer multiplication of human numbers—is precisely the measure under which its adopters, one by one, were often worse off.
item.explanation: The question falls immediately after the skeletal evidence that early farmers were shorter, more stressed and sicker, and it hands off to the answer that follows: agriculture spread "not because it made individuals healthier but because it made populations larger." It therefore marks the turn from harm-to-individuals toward an explanation of the spread that does not run through individual benefit, which is the key. The option that has the author conceding "agriculture ultimately did improve human health despite early setbacks" is the tempting misread; no such concession is made, and the passage ends by saying adopters were "often worse off." The option claiming the author "will now reject the skeletal evidence" as inconclusive gets the move backwards - that evidence is accepted and built upon. And the option in which the question "invites readers to consider foraging societies" as a preferable model imports a present-day value judgment the passage never makes its business.
item.correct_answer: It marks a turn from evidence that farming harmed individuals to an explanation of its spread that does not depend on individual benefit.

distractor_rationales.choice: It introduces the author's concession that agriculture ultimately did improve human health despite early setbacks.
It signals that the author will now reject the skeletal evidence just presented as inconclusive.
It invites readers to consider foraging societies as a model preferable to modern agriculture.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen Grüber's generalization?
choices: A blood-donation program that began offering cash payments saw its number of voluntary donors fall.
Raising the daycare fine to a very high level eventually cut late pickups below their level before any fine existed.
Parents in the daycare study reported that they strongly disliked the late fine and considered it an unfair penalty.
Factory workers paid by the piece produced substantially more units than comparable workers paid a fixed weekly salary.
item.passage: Economists once treated incentives as additive: pay people to do something and they will do more of it. Fields of evidence now complicate the axiom. When a daycare fined parents for late pickups, latenesses rose rather than fell—the fine reframed a moral lapse as a purchasable service, and parents, no longer ashamed, simply bought the extra time. Grüber generalizes the pattern: an explicit price can crowd out the unpriced norms—guilt, duty, reciprocity—that were doing the real regulatory work, so that adding a monetary incentive sometimes weakens the very behavior it targets. The lesson is not that incentives never work but that they are never merely added to a situation; they redescribe it, and the redescription can dissolve the motives a policymaker was relying on.
item.explanation: The generalization is that attaching an explicit price can crowd out unpriced norms - guilt, duty, reciprocity - so that the incentive weakens the very behavior it targets. A blood-donation program whose voluntary donors fall away after it "began offering cash payments" is a second, independent instance of that crowding out, which is what generalizing a pattern requires. The option in which "Raising the daycare fine to a very high level" eventually cuts late pickups below their pre-fine level cuts the other way: it says the price works after all, once large enough. The report that parents "considered it an unfair penalty" records an attitude, whereas the claim at issue is about behavior; disliking a fine is compatible with either outcome. And the piece-rate finding, in which workers "produced substantially more units" than salaried counterparts, is a clean illustration of the additive view of incentives that the passage is complicating.
item.correct_answer: A blood-donation program that began offering cash payments saw its number of voluntary donors fall.

distractor_rationales.choice: Raising the daycare fine to a very high level eventually cut late pickups below their level before any fine existed.
Parents in the daycare study reported that they strongly disliked the late fine and considered it an unfair penalty.
Factory workers paid by the piece produced substantially more units than comparable workers paid a fixed weekly salary.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the passage's central argument?
choices: Evidence that certain non-coding sequences regulate the expression of nearby genes
A finding that most non-coding DNA is transcribed into RNA at some point in the life of the cell, if only at low levels
A study showing that non-coding regions which are biochemically active are usually not conserved across related species
Evidence that conserved non-coding sequences rarely display any biochemical activity
item.passage: For decades the vast stretches of the genome that code for no protein were dismissed as 'junk,' evolutionary debris carried along inertly. The discovery that some of this material regulates when and how genes are expressed prompted a dramatic reversal: headlines announced that junk DNA was functional after all. The swing has gone too far. That a sequence is transcribed, or binds a protein, does not establish that it does anything the organism depends on; cells are chemically busy places, and incidental activity is cheap. The rigorous test of function is not biochemical activity but evolutionary conservation—whether natural selection has preserved a sequence against the steady drift of mutation. By that standard, a substantial fraction of non-coding DNA still shows no sign of being maintained, and is most parsimoniously read as nonfunctional. The correction to 'junk' was overdue; its wholesale reversal is not yet earned.
item.explanation: The central argument is that biochemical activity is not evidence of function and that conservation is the real test; showing active regions are typically not conserved supports exactly that decoupling. Option one supports the 'reversal' the passage warns against. Option two describes activity the passage explicitly says does not establish function—so it would be dismissed, not strengthening. Option four muddles the passage's own criterion by pitting conservation against activity in the wrong direction.
item.correct_answer: A study showing that non-coding regions which are biochemically active are usually not conserved across related species

distractor_rationales.choice: Evidence that certain non-coding sequences regulate the expression of nearby genes
A finding that most non-coding DNA is transcribed into RNA at some point
Evidence that conserved non-coding sequences rarely display any biochemical activity

item.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the sentence 'Foragers were not innocent of hierarchy; they policed it'?
choices: It concedes that foraging societies, for all their leveling techniques, were ultimately as hierarchical as the societies that followed them.
It restates the traditional claim that social hierarchy is natural and inevitable.
It crystallizes the passage's central revision: that equality was actively maintained rather than merely given.
It introduces evidence that undermines the reliability of ethnographic methods.
item.passage: Anthropologists once held up mobile foraging bands as living proof of primordial equality—societies without chiefs, hoarding, or command. The picture was a useful corrective to the assumption that hierarchy is natural and eternal. But it hardened into a myth of its own. Ethnography reveals that such 'equality' was not the absence of power but its active, effortful suppression: bands leveled would-be big men through ridicule, gossip, and the threat of desertion, techniques that presuppose the very impulses they check. Foragers were not innocent of hierarchy; they policed it. The revised view neither restores the old naturalness of rank nor preserves the romance of a hierarchy-free past. It relocates equality from a default state to an achievement—fragile, deliberate, and continually renewed.
item.explanation: The sentence lands directly after the description of leveling by 'ridicule, gossip, and the threat of desertion,' and it compresses the passage's revision: forager equality was 'not the absence of power but its active, effortful suppression.' Reading it as a concession 'that foraging societies were ultimately as hierarchical as later ones' overstates, since the passage relocates equality from a default to an achievement, not to rank. Reading it as a restatement of 'the traditional claim that social hierarchy is natural and inevitable' inverts the point: to police hierarchy is to suppress it, which is the opposite of endorsing its inevitability. And reading it as introducing 'evidence that undermines the reliability of ethnographic methods' is off-topic, since ethnography is the passage's source and never its target.
item.correct_answer: It crystallizes the passage's central revision: that equality was actively maintained rather than merely given.

It restates the traditional claim that social hierarchy is natural and inevitable.
It introduces evidence that undermines the reliability of ethnographic methods.

item.prompt: Based on Text 2, the scholars it describes would most likely characterize the praise described in Text 1 as one that
choices: mistakes a deliberately crafted impression of spontaneity for genuinely unmediated feeling.

item.passage:
Text 1: The Romantic poets are often praised for sincerity—for making the poem a direct outpouring of genuine feeling. Wordsworth's own formula, that poetry is 'the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings,' seems to license reading his lyrics as unmediated confession.

Text 2: But Wordsworth completes his phrase: poetry 'takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity.' The feeling is not transcribed in its heat; it is summoned later, contemplated, and shaped. Some scholars conclude that the prized spontaneity is itself an effect the poet constructs—that the appearance of unmediated feeling is the product of considerable craft.
item.explanation: Text 2 restores the rest of Wordsworth's formula - feeling "recollected in tranquillity," summoned later, contemplated and shaped - and reports scholars who conclude that the prized spontaneity is an effect the poet constructs. On that view the praise in Text 1 takes a crafted impression of immediacy for the real thing, which is the key. The option that the praise "correctly locates the power of the lyrics" in Wordsworth's unforced sincerity endorses precisely the reading Text 2 undercuts. The option that the praise "understates how much genuine feeling survives into the finished lyrics" points the wrong way: these scholars say the poems are more mediated than they look, not more rawly authentic. And the option that the praise "wrongly assumes that Wordsworth revised his finished lyrics far more heavily" than he did mistakes the claim for one about manuscript revision, whereas emotion recollected in tranquillity describes contemplative shaping in the making of the poem.
item.correct_answer: mistakes a deliberately crafted impression of spontaneity for genuinely unmediated feeling.

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the revisionists' specific claim as described in the passage?
choices: Across all habitat types, including undamaged ones, ecosystems holding more non-native plants supported a greater total number of animal species than comparable sites.
In sites where native pollinator populations had crashed, animal species persisted only where naturalized plants supplied an alternative food source.
In pristine forests that had never been degraded, introduced plants cut the diversity of native insects by nearly half over two decades of continuous monitoring.
Naturalized plants were found to spread more slowly in degraded habitats than in the intact communities that surround them.
item.passage: Conservationists have traditionally treated any non-native species as a threat to be eradicated. A revisionist current argues, more carefully, that the harm of an introduced species depends less on its origin than on the condition of the ecosystem it enters. In badly degraded habitats—where native pollinators have already collapsed—certain naturalized plants can sustain the fauna that would otherwise starve, functioning as ecological stopgaps. The revisionists are emphatic, however, that this is a claim about damaged systems, not a general license: in intact communities the same species frequently outcompete natives and simplify the web of interactions. Their argument thus reframes rather than dissolves the case for vigilance; it asks managers to weigh function against provenance case by case, not to abandon the distinction between native and introduced altogether. The point is conditional, and mistaking it for a blanket endorsement of non-natives inverts its logic.
item.explanation: The revisionists' claim is narrow: in degraded systems, non-natives can act as beneficial stopgaps. The key supplies precisely that—survival in collapsed habitats tied to naturalized plants. The “all habitat types… greater total” option is the blanket endorsement the revisionists explicitly disown, so it strengthens a claim they reject. The pristine-forest finding supports continued vigilance (the intact-community side), not the stopgap claim. The spread-rate finding is about dispersal speed, irrelevant to whether non-natives benefit degraded systems.

item.prompt: Based on Text 2, which choice best describes how its author would evaluate the conclusion drawn in Text 1?
choices: As correct, because individual voter ignorance necessarily invalidates democratic outcomes.
As mistaken, because voters are in fact well informed about most policy questions.
As too sweeping, since dispersed errors can offset one another under conditions Text 1 overlooks.
As irrelevant, because democratic legitimacy does not depend on the quality of decisions.
item.passage:
Text 1: Survey after survey finds voters ignorant of basic facts—who holds office, what policies cost, which branch does what. If democratic legitimacy rests on informed consent, then democracy as practiced rests on a fiction. Decisions of vast consequence are made by an electorate that could not pass a civics quiz.

Text 2: The individual voter's ignorance is real and troubling, yet it need not be decisive. When errors are scattered rather than systematic, they can cancel in the aggregate, and a crowd of ill-informed voters can still track the better option. The mechanism is fragile: it fails precisely when ignorance is biased in one direction, as propaganda can make it. Democracy is thus neither vindicated nor doomed by voter ignorance; it is rescued only under a condition—randomness of error—that cannot be assumed.
item.explanation: Text 2 accepts the ignorance Text 1 documents but denies that it settles the question: when errors are "scattered rather than systematic, they can cancel in the aggregate," so an ill-informed electorate can still track the better option. Text 1's jump from ignorant voters to a democracy resting on a fiction is therefore too sweeping. The option endorsing Text 1 as correct "because individual voter ignorance necessarily invalidates democratic outcomes" is the trap: Text 2's concession about ignorance invites agreement, but it says democracy is "neither vindicated nor doomed." The option calling Text 1 mistaken because "voters are in fact well informed about most policy questions" contradicts Text 2's own admission that the ignorance is real and troubling. And the option calling Text 1 irrelevant because "democratic legitimacy does not depend on the quality of decisions" attributes an indifference Text 2 plainly does not hold - its whole defense turns on whether the crowd tracks the better option.
item.correct_answer: As too sweeping, since dispersed errors can offset one another under conditions Text 1 overlooks.

As mistaken, because voters are in fact well informed about most policy questions.
As irrelevant, because democratic legitimacy does not depend on the quality of decisions.

item.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: raged

item.passage: By the time the rescue team finally reached the stranded hikers, the storm ______ for nearly six hours, and the only trail down the mountain lay buried under several feet of snow.
item.explanation: The narrative is in the past ('reached,' 'lay'), and the storm's action was ongoing over a span of time that ended at a specific past moment ('by the time the rescue team reached'). This earlier, continuing past action requires the past perfect progressive 'had been raging.' 'Is raging' (present) and 'has raged' (present perfect) clash with the past frame, and the simple past 'raged' fails to show that the raging preceded and led up to the team's arrival.
item.correct_answer: had been raging

has raged
